buckets.title: Projectile motion — admitted demand extensions
buckets.badge_reason: These demands require explicit model/representation changes beyond the canonical Grade9V3 first slice.

scope.covers: Five labelled extensions required by the fixed projectile stress demand: velocity from position functions, rebound energy, piecewise gravity, trajectory-through-point reasoning and linear drag.
excluded: No change to the three canonical Motion-in-2D microtopics.
No unresearched force law or collision model.
No source-question wording presented as authored teaching.

capabilities.action: Differentiate component position functions to obtain instantaneous velocity and its direction.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses v_x=dx/dt and v_y=dy/dt at one common time, then obtains direction from the signed velocity components.

capabilities.action: Translate collision energy retention into post-impact speed before applying a new projectile launch direction.
capabilities.success_criterion: Converts a kinetic-energy fraction into a speed-squared fraction, resolves the post-bounce vertical component, and computes the next maximum height.

capabilities.action: Carry the apex state across a boundary where the constant downward acceleration changes, then solve the new stage.
capabilities.success_criterion: Preserves position and horizontal velocity at the boundary and changes only the post-boundary vertical acceleration law.

capabilities.action: Use the projectile trajectory equation to impose passage through a specified point and locate the apex relative to it.
capabilities.success_criterion: Substitutes the point into the trajectory relation and uses vertical velocity or trajectory slope to decide whether the apex is before or after the point.

capabilities.action: Replace constant-horizontal-velocity projectile reasoning with the linear-drag horizontal differential equation when F=-cv.
capabilities.success_criterion: Solves m dv_x/dt=-c v_x and integrates the exponential horizontal velocity to obtain displacement.

microtopics.title: EXTENSION — instantaneous velocity direction from x(t) and y(t)
microtopics.badge_reason: The hard decision is distinguishing position direction from the tangent/velocity direction and differentiating both component functions at the same instant.
entry_assumptions: Can interpret x(t) and y(t) as one particle with one shared time.
Has introductory meaning of derivative as instantaneous rate of change.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The direction of motion at an instant comes from the tangent velocity (dx/dt, dy/dt), not from the position vector (x,y).

teaching_path.action: Identify that the requested direction is the direction of instantaneous velocity, not the direction from the origin to the particle.
teaching_path.why_valid: Velocity is the instantaneous rate of change of position; position direction answers a different question.

teaching_path.action: Differentiate x(t) and y(t) separately to obtain v_x(t) and v_y(t).
teaching_path.why_valid: Cartesian component derivatives give the components of the velocity vector.

teaching_path.action: Evaluate both velocity components at the same requested time and use their signed ratio to determine the direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The two components form one simultaneous velocity vector only at the same instant.

teaching_path.action: Compare the velocity arrow with the local tangent to the trajectory and reject any answer based only on y/x.
teaching_path.why_valid: Instantaneous velocity is tangent to the path while the position vector generally is not.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Use y/x at the requested time to get the direction of motion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does y/x describe the tangent direction or only the direction of the position vector from the origin?
misconceptions.repair: Differentiate first; use v_y/v_x for the velocity direction.

exit_task.prompt: If x=5t and y=12t-t^2, state the operations needed to find the velocity direction at t=2 s.

answer.summary: Differentiate to get v_x=5 and v_y=12-2t, evaluate both at t=2, then use the signed component ratio and quadrant.
reasoning: Use derivatives, not x and y themselves.
Evaluate both at one time.
Use the velocity components for direction.
answer.check: The resulting velocity arrow must be tangent to the path.

microtopics.research_contribution: OpenStax explicitly defines instantaneous velocity as the derivative of the position vector and gives the component derivative relations.

predict.prompt: At t=2 s, should a direction question use y/x or (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)?
predict.defensible_answer: Use (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) because the question asks for instantaneous velocity direction.

attempt.produces: A velocity-component calculation at one instant, with a tangent check.
attempt.model_response: Name velocity as the target, differentiate both position components, evaluate at the same t, then obtain the angle from the signed velocity components.

route.ask: How do x(t) and y(t) become velocity components?
Which time must both components use?

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching reveals the completed extension; reconstruction requires the learner to choose the model or representation before seeing the route.

boundary_test.prompt: If x and y are both nonzero but v_y=0, is the velocity horizontal?
boundary_test.answer: Yes. Position direction may be slanted while the instantaneous velocity is horizontal.
boundary_test.confirms: Position direction and velocity direction are distinct.

microtopics.title: EXTENSION — projectile rebound after an energy-changing impact
microtopics.badge_reason: The main trap is converting an energy fraction directly into a speed fraction instead of remembering K is proportional to v squared.
entry_assumptions: Can use the gravity-only projectile maximum-height relation after launch.
Can resolve a speed into components.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A stated kinetic-energy retention fraction acts on v^2; after the collision creates a new launch state, only that new vertical component controls the next rise height.

teaching_path.action: Treat impact as an event boundary: pre-impact projectile flight ends and a new post-impact launch state begins.
teaching_path.why_valid: An impulsive collision changes velocity over a short event and the next free-flight segment starts from the post-impact state.

teaching_path.action: Convert K_after=f K_before into v_after^2=f v_before^2 for unchanged mass.
teaching_path.why_valid: K=1/2 mv^2, so an energy fraction multiplies speed squared.

teaching_path.action: Resolve the post-bounce speed using its stated direction and use the upward component in H=v_y^2/(2g).
teaching_path.why_valid: Maximum rise after the bounce depends on the post-bounce vertical kinetic state under gravity-only flight.

teaching_path.action: Check that losing energy cannot create a rebound height inconsistent with the retained-energy fraction and vertical-component fraction.
teaching_path.why_valid: Energy and component fractions provide an independent bound on the height.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If half the kinetic energy remains, the speed becomes half.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If K is proportional to v squared, what speed-squared fraction corresponds to a 50% energy retention?
misconceptions.repair: The speed squared becomes one half; the speed becomes 1/sqrt(2) of its previous value.

exit_task.prompt: A ball keeps 64% of its kinetic energy and rebounds at an angle alpha. State the chain needed to find its new maximum height.

answer.summary: Use v_after^2=0.64 v_before^2, take v_y=v_after sin alpha, then H=v_y^2/(2g).
reasoning: Translate energy fraction to speed squared.
Resolve the new launch direction.
Use the vertical component for height.
answer.check: The result scales with 0.64 sin^2(alpha) relative to a same-speed vertical-height reference.

microtopics.research_contribution: OpenStax supplies K=1/2 mv^2; LibreTexts documents restitution/rebound-height scaling, while the source demand supplies the energy-loss event.

predict.prompt: If a collision leaves 50% of kinetic energy, does the post-collision speed become 50%?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Its speed squared becomes 50%, so speed scales by the square root.

attempt.produces: An event-boundary diagram and an energy-to-speed-squared conversion before any projectile-height calculation.
attempt.model_response: Close the first flight at impact, convert the retained energy to post-bounce speed squared, resolve the new vertical component, then use the standard height relation.

route.ask: What state begins the second flight?
route.why_this_ask: Separates the collision event from free flight.

route.ask: What quantity is proportional to kinetic energy for fixed mass?

route.why_this_ask: Reconnects to the canonical projectile model.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching reveals the completed extension; reconstruction requires the learner to choose the model or representation before seeing the route.

boundary_test.prompt: If the ball rebounds horizontally, can it gain height immediately after the collision under gravity alone?
boundary_test.answer: No. Its post-bounce vertical component is zero, so the next rise height is zero.
boundary_test.confirms: The post-impact vertical component, not total speed, sets maximum rise.

microtopics.title: EXTENSION — projectile motion when gravity changes after the apex
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must preserve the apex state and change only the post-boundary acceleration law rather than recompute the whole flight under the new gravity.
entry_assumptions: Can identify the apex by v_y=0.
Can solve vertical constant-acceleration motion from a known state.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A change in constant gravity creates two kinematic stages joined by one boundary state; position and velocity at the apex are inherited by the second stage while acceleration changes.

teaching_path.action: Split the trajectory at the apex boundary and label stage 1 with g_1 and stage 2 with g_2.
teaching_path.why_valid: The model assumption changes at one event, so one constant-acceleration equation cannot span both regions.

teaching_path.action: Use the ordinary projectile model only up to the apex to determine the apex position and horizontal velocity.
teaching_path.why_valid: Before the boundary, gravity is g_1 and horizontal acceleration is zero.

teaching_path.action: Start stage 2 from the apex with v_y=0 and downward acceleration g_2; compute the descent time from H=(1/2)g_2 t_2^2.
teaching_path.why_valid: The second stage is constant-acceleration motion with its own acceleration but inherited initial state.

teaching_path.action: Check that increasing post-apex gravity shortens only the descent portion and therefore shortens only the post-apex horizontal distance.
teaching_path.why_valid: v_x remains unchanged at the boundary while the fall time changes.
teaching_path.output: range ratio lies between apex fraction and ordinary full range for stronger gravity

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Once gravity changes at the apex, recompute the entire trajectory using the new gravity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Did the projectile experience g_2 before it reached the apex?
misconceptions.repair: No. Preserve the stage-1 apex state, then apply g_2 only to stage 2.

exit_task.prompt: If post-apex gravity is four times larger, how does the descent time from the same apex height compare with the ordinary descent time?

answer.summary: It is half as long because t is proportional to 1/sqrt(g) for a fall from rest through the same height.
reasoning: The apex height is already fixed by stage 1.
Stage 2 starts with v_y=0.
t=sqrt(2H/g_2).
answer.check: Stronger gravity must reduce, not increase, the descent time.

microtopics.research_contribution: OpenStax establishes the standard constant-gravity projectile component model; the extension applies the same constant-acceleration relation piecewise after an explicit model boundary.

predict.prompt: When gravity changes only after the apex, which parts of the state must be carried across unchanged?
predict.defensible_answer: The apex position and velocity are continuous; the acceleration law changes after the boundary.

attempt.produces: A two-stage event line with the apex state written once and reused.
attempt.model_response: Solve stage 1 to the apex, copy the apex state, replace only the post-apex acceleration, then solve stage 2.

route.ask: What state is continuous across that boundary?
Which equation determines the new descent time?

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching reveals the completed extension; reconstruction requires the learner to choose the model or representation before seeing the route.

boundary_test.prompt: If g_2 equals g_1, should the two-stage result reduce to the ordinary projectile result?
boundary_test.confirms: The extension contains the standard model as a limiting case.

microtopics.title: EXTENSION — trajectory equation through a specified point
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must eliminate time without losing the physical event interpretation, then use the sign of vertical velocity or local slope to locate the apex.
entry_assumptions: Can write x(t) and y(t) for a gravity-only projectile.
Can resolve an initial speed into horizontal and vertical components.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Eliminating the common time creates a path equation y(x), but passing through a point and locating the apex are separate decisions.

teaching_path.action: Confirm the gravity-only projectile assumptions before eliminating time.
teaching_path.why_valid: The trajectory equation is a consequence of the standard projectile model, not a universal curve.

teaching_path.action: Use x=u cos(theta)t to eliminate t from y=u sin(theta)t-(1/2)gt^2.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both component equations describe the same event time, so eliminating that common t is valid.

teaching_path.action: Substitute the specified point coordinates to constrain u and theta.
teaching_path.why_valid: A point lies on the trajectory only if its coordinates satisfy the path equation.

teaching_path.action: Use v_y at the point or the local trajectory slope to decide whether the projectile is rising or falling there.
teaching_path.why_valid: Passing through P does not by itself reveal whether P occurs before or after the apex.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If a point satisfies the trajectory equation, the apex must be after that point.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can a projectile pass through the same height on both its rising and falling branches?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. Use v_y or slope at the point to determine the branch.

exit_task.prompt: What two checks are needed when asked whether a projectile passes through P and has already crossed its apex there?

answer.summary: First impose P in the trajectory equation; then use v_y or local slope at P to determine whether the path is descending.
reasoning: Point membership and branch are separate.
Use the trajectory equation for membership.
Use velocity/slope for apex position.
answer.check: A negative local slope or v_y indicates the apex is already behind the projectile.

microtopics.research_contribution: OpenStax derives the projectile trajectory equation by eliminating time from the component equations.

predict.prompt: Does substituting a point into y(x) alone tell you whether the projectile is rising or falling there?
predict.defensible_answer: No. It shows the point is on the path; a velocity or slope sign is still needed.

attempt.produces: A point constraint plus an independent branch/apex check.
attempt.model_response: License the projectile model, eliminate the common time, substitute the point, then inspect v_y or slope to locate the apex relative to the point.

route.why_this_ask: Keeps model choice ahead of algebra.
Connects y(x) back to x(t), y(t).

route.ask: How do you determine the branch at P?
route.why_this_ask: Separates point membership from apex position.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching reveals the completed extension; reconstruction requires the learner to choose the model or representation before seeing the route.

boundary_test.prompt: If tan(theta)=y_P/x_P exactly, can a finite-speed gravity-only projectile launched from the origin pass through P above the straight launch ray?
boundary_test.answer: No. Gravity lowers the path below the straight-line term for any finite speed.
boundary_test.confirms: The gravity term imposes a physical reachability constraint.

microtopics.title: EXTENSION — projectile motion with linear drag
microtopics.badge_reason: The key model decision is recognizing that velocity-dependent drag makes acceleration non-constant, so the ordinary constant-acceleration projectile formulas no longer apply.
entry_assumptions: Can apply Newton's second law to one component.
Understands an exponential decay law at a qualitative level or can follow its supplied solution.
microtopics.inferential_jump: With F_drag=-cv, horizontal acceleration is proportional to -v_x rather than zero; solving the differential equation gives exponential velocity decay and displacement must be integrated from that velocity.

teaching_path.action: Reject the standard a_x=0 projectile specialization when linear drag F=-cv is retained.
teaching_path.why_valid: Drag has a horizontal component whenever v_x is nonzero, so horizontal acceleration is not zero.

teaching_path.action: Write Newton's second law in x: m dv_x/dt=-c v_x.
teaching_path.why_valid: Linear drag opposes the instantaneous velocity and is proportional to its component.

teaching_path.action: Use the exponential solution v_x(t)=v_x0 exp(-ct/m) and integrate it over time.
teaching_path.why_valid: The first-order decay equation has an exponential solution; displacement is the time integral of velocity.

teaching_path.action: Check that c→0 recovers x-x_0≈v_x0 t and that drag distance is smaller than the no-drag distance for c>0.
teaching_path.why_valid: The limiting model and inequality provide independent checks.
teaching_path.output: solution recovers no-drag limit and reduced range

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Use x=v_x0 t because projectile horizontal velocity is always constant.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the drag force has an x component -c v_x, can a_x still be zero?
misconceptions.repair: No. Solve the velocity-dependent equation first, then integrate v_x(t).

exit_task.prompt: For m dv_x/dt=-c v_x, state v_x(t), the horizontal displacement from 0 to t, and one limiting check.

answer.summary: v_x=v_x0 e^{-ct/m}; Δx=(m/c)v_x0(1-e^{-ct/m}); as c approaches zero, Δx approaches v_x0 t.
reasoning: Solve the linear decay equation.
Integrate velocity.
Check the zero-drag limit.
answer.check: For positive c and t, the distance is less than v_x0 t.

microtopics.research_contribution: OpenStax describes the linear-drag regime and solves the corresponding exponential velocity response; the source demand applies the same law to the horizontal projectile component.

predict.prompt: If drag is proportional to velocity, may you still use the ordinary constant-horizontal-velocity projectile shortcut?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Drag makes a_x depend on v_x, so horizontal velocity decays.

attempt.produces: A model-choice statement, horizontal ODE, exponential velocity law and integrated displacement.
attempt.model_response: Write Newton II for the horizontal component, solve the exponential decay, integrate to displacement, and verify against the no-drag limit.

route.why_this_ask: Prevents multiplying final velocity by time.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching reveals the completed extension; reconstruction requires the learner to choose the model or representation before seeing the route.

boundary_test.prompt: If c is extremely small, what should the drag result resemble?
boundary_test.answer: The ordinary no-drag horizontal motion x≈v_x0 t.
boundary_test.confirms: The modified model joins smoothly to the canonical model.

question_families.title: Projectile modified-dynamics and representation-demand extensions
solution_structure: Start from the canonical component/projectile model.
Identify the explicit demand change and the event/model boundary.
Select the admitted extension relation before algebra.
Preserve one frame and one clock across component work.
Check the result against a canonical limit or physical bound.

demand_dimensions.model_choice: Decide when the standard projectile model must be replaced or applied piecewise.
demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Translate position laws, component ratios, point constraints or decay observations into the taught extension representation.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Preserve event state across impact/apex boundaries and sequence the new relation before canonical consequences.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Change the demand structure while using only extensions explicitly taught in this product.

safe_variations: Change numerical values without changing the model.

questions.stem: A projectile launched at 45° reaches 80 m maximum height. On returning to the ground it retains 60% of its kinetic energy and rebounds at 30° above horizontal. Find its new maximum height.
conditions: Ground is level.

Post-bounce v_y^2=192g×sin^2 30°=48g, so H'=48g/(2g)=24 m.

reasoning_route.action: Check energy/component scaling bounds.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Loss and smaller vertical fraction must reduce height.

questions.stem: A projectile launched at 45° passes through P=(4 m,1 m). Find u²/g and decide whether the projectile is rising or falling at P.

questions.stem: A projectile's measured horizontal velocity halves every τ seconds in a medium. Decide whether x=v_x0 t is valid and write a horizontal displacement expression in terms of v_x0, τ and t consistent with linear drag.
